title: Cybernetic Prodigy?
text:
Throughout history, child prodigies have captivated our imagination and reminded us of the remarkable capacities of human intelligence. Mozart composed his first symphony at eight years old. Picasso mastered academic painting techniques before adolescence. Garry Kasparov became a chess grandmaster at sixteen. These extraordinary individuals achieved what most accomplish only after decades of practice, if at all, demonstrating the seemingly infinite possibilities of human potential across generations.
What unites these prodigies is their early mastery of specific domains—whether mathematics, art, music, or sport. Their achievements stem from an incomparable level of curiosity and tenacity, an insatiable drive to inquire, understand, and discover within their chosen field. Yet when we survey the landscape of human achievement, one field appears conspicuously absent from the pantheon of prodigies: cybernetics. This absence is not accidental. It reveals something fundamental about the nature of cybernetic thinking itself.


Cybernetics, as defined by Norbert Wiener, is the science of communication and control in animals and machines. W. Ross Ashby further developed this framework to understand how systems regulate themselves through feedback mechanisms. However, these definitions only hint at the true scope of the field. Cybernetics is fundamentally concerned with patterns that recur across vastly different domains—the feedback loop that governs a thermostat operates on the same principle as homeostasis in living organisms, the self-correction mechanisms in ecosystems, and the regulatory dynamics within social organisations.
This interdisciplinary synthesis represents cybernetics’ greatest strength and its distinguishing characteristic. The field does not merely borrow from multiple disciplines; it seeks the meta-level patterns that connect them. A cybernetician must recognise how information flows through biological neural networks and economic markets, how control systems operate in both mechanical devices and political institutions, how the same principles of circular causality emerge in contexts as diverse as molecular biology and organisational behaviour.
When we examine the intellectual development of foundational cyberneticians like Wiener and Ashby, we discover a pattern. Their “cybernetic sensitivity” emerged not from early singular focus but from accumulated exposure to diverse systems throughout their formative years and professional lives. Wiener’s background spanned mathematics, philosophy, and engineering. Ashby trained as a physician before developing his theories of self-organising systems. Their insights arose from recognising patterns across their varied experiences—connections that became apparent only after extensive engagement with multiple domains.
This reveals why cybernetics resists the phenomenon of prodigy-hood. The field demands a particular kind of abstraction that requires extensive exposure to diverse systems over time. A child might demonstrate remarkable technical precocity—building sophisticated robots or mastering control theory mathematics—but this represents engineering skill and mathematical logic rather than genuine cybernetic insight. True cybernetic understanding means seeing the thermostat and the cell membrane as instantiations of the same regulatory principle, recognising the feedback dynamics in a predator-prey relationship and a corporate hierarchy as fundamentally related phenomena. This meta-level pattern recognition across radically different contexts appears to require what only time can provide: breadth of experience, cognitive maturity to think in cross-domain analogies, and observation of how systems behave over extended timescales.
The very nature of cybernetics—as a relational and contextual discipline—makes it incompatible with early mastery. Where mathematics offers abstract structures that can be grasped in isolation, and music provides clear performance metrics within a bounded domain, cybernetics asks us to understand relationships, contexts, and the patterns that connect seemingly unrelated phenomena. It is a discipline that inherently favours the synthesiser, the integrator, the thinker who connects dots across years of accumulated experience with different kinds of systems.



People often ask me: What is cybernetics?
The question resists simple answers, though I remain partial to Wiener’s elegant formulation that cybernetics is the science of communication and control. Yet this definition, like all attempts to capture the field in one or two sentences, feels incomplete. Cybernetics is inherently philosophical in character, resistant to being confined within neat definitional boundaries.
The field is certainly broad, but its breadth alone does not fully characterise it. The true depth of cybernetics emerges from its recognition and conceptualisation of universal patterns across systems and domains—order arising from randomness, resilience grown from perturbations and noise, stability maintained through constant feedback mechanisms operating beneath the surface of apparent complexity. These patterns reveal themselves not through narrow focus but through wide-ranging observation and reflection.
Consider the parallel to other profound questions. Tell me about mother. Tell me what physics is. These questions, like “What is cybernetics?”, cannot be adequately answered in brief. They point towards understanding that unfolds through engagement and experience rather than through definition alone.
Perhaps, then, we must reframe our enquiry. Rather than asking “What is cybernetics?” or wondering why we find no cybernetics prodigies, we might better ask: Where can I start to understand cybernetics?
It is worth remembering that cybernetics emerged in the post-war era, born from the collaborative efforts of scientists, mathematicians, engineers, and social scientists who sought to apply human knowledge towards the betterment of humanity. The early cyberneticians gathered at the Macy Conferences not as isolated specialists but as interdisciplinary thinkers committed to shared understanding. This origin speaks to something essential about the field’s character: cybernetics is fundamentally inclusive and participatory. It welcomes diverse perspectives and recognises that insight emerges from dialogue across different ways of knowing. The field does not demand credentials or gatekeep access to its ideas; rather, it invites anyone willing to observe patterns, think systemically, and engage with the profound questions of how systems communicate, regulate, and evolve.
The answer to where one might begin lies not in early specialisation or isolated mastery, but in cultivating breadth of experience, attending to patterns across domains, and developing the patience to let systems thinking mature over time. Cybernetics, it turns out, teaches us something important about expertise itself—that some forms of understanding cannot be rushed, and that the deepest insights often come to those who have learnt to see connections across the full landscape of their accumulated experience.
Gregory Bateson, one of the most profound cybernetic thinkers, once wrote that “the pattern which connects is a meta-pattern. It is a pattern of patterns.” Perhaps this is why there are no cybernetics prodigies. The field asks us not merely to master a domain, but to perceive the meta-pattern—to recognise the threads that weave through the thermostat and the cell, the forest and the market, the individual mind and the collective whole. Such vision cannot be taught in childhood; it must be lived into being, pattern by pattern, connection by connection, across the full arc of a curious life.
Still wondering what cybernetics is? Well, come on and let’s go find patterns from the world first!

title: Emergence & Hopeful Futures for Hong Kong Baptist University Study Tour
text: As part of the Hong Kong Baptist University Global Study Tour hosted by the ANU McCusker Institute, I ran a session entitled Emergence and Hopeful Futures: Beauty of Self-organisation to inspire students with the priniciples of self-organisation that is pivotal in endowing many systems in nature and society with adaptability and resilience under constant changes. This was a compact version, condensed to fit in an hour-long session from the original duration of 2.5hr-long, as a recurring workshop in each semester as part of the McCusker Institute’s SoCIETIE program.

title: Global Mathematics Histories and Futures
text:
Entitled “From clockwork to complexity: Tracing the evolution of our worldviews with mathematics”, I contributed to two guest lectures to trace the evolution of mathematics from describing a predictable mechanical universe to understanding adaptive, self-organising, and interconnected systems. Beginning with mechanical philosophy and Newtonian determinism, the lecture traces the emergence of cybernetics, information theory, and complexity science through ideas of feedback, entropy, and emergence. Drawing on diverse examples ranging from autonomous machines to hyperuniform structures and generative AI, the lecture reflects on evolving mathematical worldviews for understanding complex organisation across natural, technological, and social systems.
The workshop was convened by Prof. Rowena Ball.

title: Santa Fe Institute Complex Systems Summer School 2024
text:
Santa Fe Institute Complex Systems Summer School (CSSS) 2024 consists of a series of lectures and workshops devoted to theory and tools in complexity science, applications-focused seminars, and discussions with faculty and fellow participants on diverse topics, such as economics, evolutionary theory, natural language processing, networks, nonlinear dynamics and scaling theory. I was one of only 40 participants globally selected for the program from the pool of 175+ applicants (<23% selection rate).
CSSS participants are expected to put what they learn from these didactic sessions into practice through group research projects, conducted throughout the program and often extending into manuscripts and longer-term collaborations.

title: Sungyeon Hong
Sungyeon Hong
text:
Complexity · Information · Topology
  Research
  
    
        We are living in a vast ocean of data. As cognitive beings, we continually seek to derive meaning from the information we encounter — identifying patterns, forming abstractions, and constructing narratives that help us navigate an increasingly complex world.
    
    
      My research asks a simple yet far-reaching question: how do coherent structures emerge from many interacting components without central control? From material organisation and communication networks to embodied human experience, I investigate how local interactions give rise to collective patterns, adaptive behaviours, and shared meaning.
    
    
      Beginning with my PhD work on geometry-driven hyperuniformity, I became interested in how remarkably simple generative rules can produce striking forms of collective order. More recently, I have extended this perspective to information systems mediated by generative AI, where feedback, adaptation, and communication continually reshape how knowledge is created, circulated, and transformed. Alongside these computational studies, I am exploring embodied complexity through interactive experiences, such as Musical Allostasis, which invites participants to experience self-organisation and collective dynamics through collaborative music-making, with feedback and feedforward anticipation shaping how the group adapts over time.
    
    
        Across these domains, I combine ideas from complexity science, cybernetics, and topology to uncover organisational principles that transcend individual systems. Rather than studying any single application in isolation, I seek recurring structures and mechanisms that reveal how complex systems organise, adapt, and remain resilient across diverse domains.
    
  



  
    Research themes
    
        Click on each research theme below to find more details.
    
    
      
        
        
          Order, Disorder and In-between
          How simple local interactions generate spatial organisation and reveal universal principles of pattern formation.
        
      

      
        
        
          Information Dynamics
          How information, meaning, and knowledge evolve through communication, feedback, and human–AI interaction.
        
      

      
        
        
          Embodied Complexity
          How self-organisation, adaptation, and collective behaviour can be experienced through interactive systems and creative media.

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
Teaching · Supervision · Mentoring
        Education
        
          
          Education has always been close to my heart. As the eldest in my family, I grew up helping my two younger brothers with various subjects, through which I gained valuable perspectives on education. Beyond the familiar, funny sibling dynamic (often involving fiery arguments over seemingly nothing, clashes of opinions, and, sometimes, dramatic retelling of events to our parents), those moments taught me that learning is as much about connections and relationships as it is about knowledge.
          
          
                
                Supporting my first (and most adorable) students shaped my educational philosophy from an early age. It convinced me that the most meaningful learning emerges when curiosity leads the way, students take a proactive role in their own learning, and the process remains enjoyable. Since then, I have sought to cultivate learning environments that are curiosity-driven, student-led, and centred on the joy of discovery.
                
          
    
        
    

    
        Educational approach
        
            My teaching draws on cybernetics, complexity, and hands-on learning to help students engage critically and creatively with the systems that shape our world.
          Across undergraduate, postgraduate, and non-award courses, I aim to create learning environments where students can move between conceptual understanding, practical experimentation, and reflective engagement with real-world complexity.
        

        
          
            Systems
            Cybernetic thinking
            Rather than focusing solely on individual parts, cybernetic thinking encourages us to understand the patterns of interaction in a system that give rise to collective behaviour and emergent outcomes, helping learners develop a richer understanding of interconnected systems.
          

          
            Dialogue
            Cross-disciplinarity
            I am particularly interested in exploring universal patterns and ideas that transcend disciplinary boundaries, creating opportunities for conversations that connect different ways of knowing and broaden our understanding of the complex world we inhabit.
          
          
          
            Practice
            Learning by making
            Students learn by building, testing, prototyping, and reflecting. I use hands-on activities to help learners encounter complexity not as an abstract idea, but as something they can observe, manipulate, and reason with.
          
        
    

    
        
          Teaching engagements
          
            My teaching engagement spans undergraduate, postgraduate, and non-award courses at ANU. The examples below highlight courses and learning experiences where I contribute to conceptual framing, facilitation, hands-on inquiry, and reflective learning design.
          

          
            
              Postgraduate teaching · ANU School of Cybernetics
              
                Master of Applied Cybernetics
                    
              I am teaching in CYBN8001: Building Cyber-Physical Systems I & II (24 units), a core year-long course in the Master of Applied Cybernetics. This course enables students to critically analyse emerging technological constellations and engage in informed conversations about cybernetic systems. Grounded in a learning-by-making ethos, the course supports students as they design and build cyber-physical system prototypes both individually and in diverse collaborative teams.
              
                Postgraduate
                Cyber-physical systems
                Studio learning
              
            

            
              Non-award courses · ANU School of Cybernetics
              
                Learning Experiences
              
              
              As part of the School's Navigating Cybernetic Futures Learning Experience (LX) series, I contribute to the delivery of a one-day non-award module, Decoding/Leading AI through Cybernetics. Working within a presenter team, I help equip participants from industry, government, and community sectors with clearer ways of understanding AI as part of wider social, cultural, economic, and ecological systems.
              
              
                Non-award
                AI literacy
                Professional education
              
            

            
              Undergraduate teaching · ANU McCusker Institute
              SoCIETIE Initiatives
              
              As a SoCIETIE Affiliate at the ANU McCusker Institute, I develop and facilitate undergraduate workshops called KNoTs (Know the Nature of Things) within the Cybernetics for Social Impact curriculum, which was awarded Transdisciplinary Teaching Award 2026. The aim of the workshops is to equip students with transdisciplinary tools and systems perspectives for engaging with complex social issues, imagining hopeful futures, and creating meaningful impact.

        Research supervision and mentoring
        
          My supervision and mentoring practice is grounded in curiosity, care, and methodological openness. I am interested in supporting students whose projects engage with complexity, cybernetics, information dynamics, topology, AI-mediated systems, or related questions about emergence and knowledge systems.
        

        
          
            Research supervision
            I welcome projects that combine conceptual, computational, empirical, or design-oriented approaches to understanding complex systems.
          

          
            Mentoring
            Inspired by a pay-it-forward ethos, I aim to help students and emerging researchers clarify their questions, navigate uncertainty, and develop confidence in transdisciplinary work.
          

          
            Possible project directions
            
              Modelling complex systems to deepen our understanding of pattern formation and the emergence of collective behaviour

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
← Research Overview
  Pattern formation · Emergent order ·  Hyperuniformity
  
    
        
    


Nature rarely presents us with perfect order or complete randomness. Snowflakes and crystals are highly ordered; gases and crowds may appear almost random. Yet many of the most intriguing systems inhabit the rich territory between these extremes, where simple local interactions give rise to complex collective organisation. Understanding this interplay offers insights not only into physical materials but also into biological, social, and technological systems that continually organise and reorganise themselves.
My research in this area began with geometry-driven hyperuniformity, where I investigated how simple geometric interactions among neighbouring points spontaneously generate large-scale order without any central coordination. This work revealed how topological defects, orientational domains, and scale-free correlations emerge during ordering transitions towards hyperuniformity, leading to unusual structural and mechanical properties.
Today, these ideas continue to motivate my broader interest in emergence, phase transitions, and universality across complex systems. By combining geometry, topology, computation, and dynamical modelling, I seek common organising principles that transcend individual disciplines — from condensed matter and biological tissues to collective behaviour and adaptive systems.

“What is order? Order was usually considered as a wonderful building, a loss of uncertainty. Typically it means that if a system is so constructed that if you know the location or the property of one element, you can make conclusions about the other elements. So order is essentially the arrival of redundancy in a system, a reduction of possibilities.”

— Heinz von Foerster, Understanding Understanding (2003)








  Below is a list of publications connected to my work on geometry-driven hyperuniformity, pattern formation, local relaxation, and emergent order.

  
  
    
      
                
            
      
        
            
        
        
          Authors: Sungyeon Hong, Mohammad Saadatfar
          Year: 2025
          Publisher: Data-Driven Modelling: Unravelling Complexity in the Sea of Data
        
        
          This work investigates how large-scale order can emerge from simple local interactions. Using a computational process known as Lloyd's algorithm, we show that a disordered collection of points can self-organise into a hyperuniform state characterised by orientational domains whose sizes grow with the system itself. The absence of a characteristic length scale suggests a form of scale-free organisation, a hallmark of systems capable of coordinated collective responses across many scales.
        
      
    

    
      
                
            
      
        
            
        
        
          Authors: Sungyeon Hong, Can Nerse, Sebastian Oberst, Mohammad Saadatfar
          Year: 2024
          Publisher: PNAS Nexus
        
        
          Can disorder be engineered to produce useful physical behaviour? In this study, we reveal how topological defects that emerge during the formation of hyperuniform structures give rise to distinct mechanical states capable of localising vibrational energy. By connecting geometry, topology, and mechanics, this work demonstrates how robust functional properties can arise from self-organising disordered materials.
        
      
    
    
    
      
                
            
      
        
            
        
        
          Authors: Sungyeon Hong, Michael A. Klatt, Gerd Schröder-Turk, Nicolas François, and Mohammad Saadatfar
          Year: 2021
          Conference: Powders & Grains 2021 – 9th International Conference on Micromechanics on Granular Media
        
        
          This paper explores how topological defects evolve during the formation of hyperuniform structures. We show that as the system becomes increasingly ordered, defects slow down and eventually become trapped, leaving a characteristic structural signature. The results provide insight into how local topological processes shape the emergence of large-scale order in complex systems.

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
← Research Overview
  Information · Meaning · Adaptation
  Information dynamics
  
    How does information evolve as it moves through complex communication networks?
  




  Overview
  
    Information rarely remains unchanged as it passes from one person (or a system) to another. Meanings are interpreted, compressed, transformed, and occasionally distorted through continual interaction. As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in how we create, communicate, and evaluate knowledge, understanding these dynamics has become both a scientific and societal challenge.
  
  
  This research theme examines how information evolves when humans and AI systems communicate and interact. I am interested in generative AI not merely as a technological artefact, but as part of a broader information ecosystem that shapes how knowledge is produced, circulated, interpreted, and transformed.
    
    
    My current work investigates semantic dynamics in recursive human–AI communication using tools from topology, geometry, and network science. By analysing trajectories of meaning across multimodal AI systems and large-scale knowledge networks, I seek to develop quantitative diagnostics for semantic drift, information flow, and knowledge integrity. Ultimately, this research aims to identify structural signatures that distinguish resilient knowledge ecosystems from those vulnerable to fragmentation, misinformation, or epistemic degradation, providing foundations for more trustworthy and responsible human–AI collaboration.
  





  
    Relevant publications
    
      Below is a list of publications connected to my work on human–AI interaction, communication, feedback, adaptation, and information dynamics.
      
    

    
    
      
        
            
        
        
            
            Semantic topologies in the recursive application of generative AI models↗
          
          
            Authors: Ben Swift, Sungyeon Hong
            Year: 2026
            Conference: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
          
          
            Generative AI systems increasingly communicate not only with humans but also with other AI systems. This study investigates what happens when information is repeatedly translated between text and images by different generative models. Using clustering and topological data analysis, we show how semantic meaning drifts, stabilises, or transforms through recursive AI-mediated communication, offering new ways to study information dynamics in complex AI ecosystems.
          
        
      

      
            
                        
                
        
            
            A scenario-based design pack for exploring multimodal human–GenAI relations↗
          
          
            Authors: Josh Andres, Chris Danta, Andrea Bianchi, Sahar Farzanfar, Gloria Milena Fernandez-Nieto, Alexa Becker, Tara Capel, Frances Liddell, Shelby Hagemann, Ned Cooper, Sungyeon Hong, Li Lin, Eduardo Benitez Sandoval, Anna Brynskov, Hubert Dariusz Zając, Zhuying Li, Tianyi Zhang, Arngeir Berge
            Year: 2025
            Publisher: Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Multimodal Interaction
          
          
            As generative AI becomes embedded in everyday life, understanding its broader social and relational impacts becomes increasingly important. This work introduces a practical design toolkit that helps researchers, designers, and students explore future human–AI relationships through scenario-building and critical reflection. The resulting framework encourages more responsible and context-aware approaches to emerging AI technologies.
          
        
      
      
      
        
            
        
        
            
            Understanding and shaping human-technology assemblages in the age of generative AI↗
          
          
            Authors: Josh Andres, Chris Danta, Andrea Bianchi, Sungyeon Hong, Zhuying Li, Eduardo Benitez Sandoval, Charles Patrick Martin, Ned Cooper
            Year: 2024
            Conference: 2024 ACM Designing Interactive Systems Conference
          
          
            Generative AI should be understood not merely as a tool, but as part of larger human–technology–environment systems. Bringing together researchers and practitioners from diverse disciplines, the project explored methods for imagining and shaping possible futures of human–AI interaction. It laid the conceptual foundations for subsequent work on Human–GenAI relations and sociotechnical design.

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
← Research Overview
        Embodiment · Collective dynamics · Equilibrium
        Embodied complexity
        
          Can we experience complexity, rather than merely observe it?
        
    


    
        Overview
        
          Complex systems are often introduced through equations, simulations, and abstract models. While these are indispensable scientific tools, they can sometimes obscure the intuitive experience of emergence itself. I am interested in designing interactive systems that allow people to participate in complexity — not simply by watching patterns unfold, but by becoming part of the dynamics that generate them and using their own sensory apparatus.
        

        
          My work in embodied complexity explores how ideas from cybernetics, complexity science, and self-organisation can be experienced through physical interaction, collaborative activities, and creative media. Rather than treating participants as passive observers, these projects invite them to become interacting agents whose local decisions collectively shape global outcomes.
        
        
          Current projects include Musical Allostasis, an interactive framework in which participants create a collective soundscape through local listening, anticipation and adaptation, together with a growing collection of online demonstrations that explore pattern formation, emergence, and adaptive systems. Through these activities, I hope to make complex systems more tangible, accessible, and enjoyable while opening new opportunities for research, education, and public engagement.

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
← Embodied Complexity
  Self-organisation · Collective dynamic · Embodying cybernetics
  Musical Allostasis
  
    How might a collective musical system adapt not only to what it hears now, but also to what it anticipates next?
  

  
    Exploratory
    Interactive
    Participatory
  




  Overview

  
    One of the recurring questions throughout my research is how collective order emerges without a central controller — a phenomenon known as self-organisation. Whether in materials, ecosystems, communication networks, or human–AI systems, complex patterns often arise from simple local interactions among many individual components. While these ideas are commonly illustrated through simulations of particles, cells, or agents, I have been interested in exploring whether they can also be experienced directly through music.
  

  
    The project began with the idea of homeostasis, inspired in part by W. Ross Ashby's Homeostat: an early cybernetic machine demonstrating how stable global behaviour can emerge through continual local adjustment. This provided the initial motivation for turning self-organisation into a shared musical experience. Yet homeostasis can also imply maintaining or returning to a relatively fixed state, whereas the dynamics I am interested in are often more open-ended: participants respond to what they hear, anticipate how the collective sound may develop, and continually revise their actions as the situation changes.
  

  
    For this reason, I now describe the project as Musical Allostasis. In physiology and complex adaptive systems, allostasis broadly refers to achieving stability through change. Rather than merely correcting deviations after they occur, an allostatic system can also act in anticipation of changing conditions. In Musical Allostasis, this distinction opens space for both feedback — responding to the sound that already exists — and feedforward — acting on expectations about where the collective soundscape may be heading.
  

  
    Music provides a way to feel adaptation in motion: we listen to one another, anticipate change, and collectively shape a soundscape that no individual determines alone.
  

  
    Preprint

    
        Hong, S., & Wong, P. (2026). Musical Allostasis: Foundations of an Embodied Cybernetic Research Programme (Version 0.1). Zenodo. 
        
        https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22686798
        
    



    
      Read the preprint →
    
  





  
    Why music?

      
        
          I was very fortunate to grow up in an environment filled with music. My musical journey began when I started learning the piano at the age of seven — after being turned away a year earlier by my prospective piano teacher simply because I was "too young"(!). After a few years, as a teenager, I managed to convince my parents that I absolutely needed a violin in my life, and later I picked up a guitar in my 20s so I could accompany myself while singing.
        

        
          Music for me
          
            Music grounds me, lifts me, and reminds me that connection can exist beyond words and equations.
          
        

        
          My favourite downtime is with singing at the top of my lungs, simply for the joy and comfort it brings. Music has become an indispensable part of my life. It grounds me, lifts me up, and creates beautiful resonance across space and time.
        
        
          What fascinates me most is music's remarkable ability to connect people. Even without formal musical training or verbal communication, music invites us to be present and, in many ways, to recognise something about ourselves. We may not share the same language, technical vocabulary, or cultural background, yet we can still sense tension and release, harmony and imbalance, repetition and change through our sensory apparatus. In those shared experiences, music becomes more than sound — it becomes a way of relating to one another and, more importantly, of making meaning together.
        

        
          Central idea
          
            What if musical coherence emerged not from a composer, but from everyone listening, anticipating, adapting, and responding together?
          
        

        
          Musical Allostasis therefore shifts attention away from musical expertise and towards listening, anticipation, adaptation, and collective sense-making. Participants do not perform a predetermined composition; instead, they continually shape the conditions in which a collective musical structure can emerge, persist, and reorganise.
        
      


  




  How Musical Allostasis works
  
    In its simplest form, Musical Allostasis (MA) v0.1 translates four elements of an adaptive collective system into a shared musical activity.
  

  
    
      01
      Initial condition
      
        Each participant begins by selecting an arbitrary sustained note. The group therefore starts from a deliberately uncoordinated musical state.
      
    

    
      02
      Feedback
      
        Participants listen to the surrounding sound and may change their own note at any time. Their actions are shaped by the collective musical state that already exists.
      
    

    
      03
      Feedforward
      
        Participants may also act in anticipation — sensing where the soundscape appears to be heading and adjusting before a stable pattern has fully formed.
      
    

    
      04
      Collective reorganisation
      
        Through repeated mutual adjustment, the group may settle temporarily into a coherent configuration, move between several such configurations, or reorganise when disturbed. The focus is not a single equilibrium, but stability achieved through continual change.
      
    
  

  
    Self-organisation
    Collective dynamics
    Feedback
    Feedforward
    Anticipation
    Adaptation
    Allostasis
  






  
    Interactive experience
            
            The online version of Musical Allostasis makes the participatory activity easier to experience across classrooms, workshops, and informal gatherings. Using their own devices, participants can listen, anticipate, and adapt to one another in real time, exploring how a collective soundscape emerges and reorganises without a conductor or predetermined score.
            
    
      
        Musical Allostasis v0.1 Digital Edition
        Listen and adapt — let the music reorganise itself
        
          Invite at least two friends or colleagues to join from their own devices. Each person chooses a note, listens to the collective sound, and changes notes as the group explores a coherent musical configuration. Rather than aiming for one prescribed endpoint, pay attention to how the group adjusts, anticipates, and reorganises over time.
        
        
          No musical background is required. For the clearest experience, participate in the same physical room and keep device volumes moderate.
        

        
          Launch the Digital Edition →
        
      

      
        E
        G
        B♭
        ♪
      
    
  




  Where the project could go next
  
    Musical Allostasis is intentionally minimal at this stage. Its simplicity makes the central dynamics visible, but it also leaves substantial room for richer models: new interaction rules, computational agents, spatial or networked arrangements, multimodal visualisations, empirical studies of group behaviour, and installations that connect physical and online participation.
  
  
    I am especially interested in how different rules and constraints shape the collective configurations a group can sustain, how participants anticipate and respond to disturbances, and whether recurring dynamical signatures can be identified across different groups and settings. More broadly, the project asks whether musical interaction can provide a useful experimental and educational medium for studying how adaptive systems maintain coherence while continually changing.
  

  
    
      Collaborate
      Help develop the next iteration
      
        I would be delighted to hear from researchers, musicians, educators, designers, artists, and creative technologists interested in developing more sophisticated models, participatory experiments, interactive installations, or learning activities inspired by Musical Allostasis.

title: Sungyeon Hong
text:
FAQ · Orientation · Small human details
  Frequently Asked Questions
  
    
          
          In this page, I listed out a few common questions about my research, teaching, supervision, and me as a human.
    It is intended as a lightweight orientation point for students, collaborators, event organisers, and anyone curious about how my work connects across cybernetics, complexity, AI, and topology.
            
        
  




Research


What connects your different research interests?


Although my research spans materials, information systems, and interactive experiences, it is guided by a common question: How do coherent patterns emerge from many interacting components without central control? Whether I am studying geometry-driven complexity, information dynamics, or embodied experiences of emergence, I am ultimately interested in understanding how structure, meaning, and collective behaviour arise through local interactions. Rather than viewing these as separate disciplines, I see them as different manifestations of the same underlying principles of complexity.





Why do you work across such different fields?

    
    I've never been particularly good at fitting neatly into a single disciplinary box. Although I was trained in mathematics and physics, I have always found myself following questions rather than labels. If the same question appears in materials science, ecology, communication, music, or AI, I'm naturally inclined to explore all of them.
    
    
    Many of these seemingly different systems are connected by common ideas, such as emergence, self-organisation, feedback, adaptation, and collective behaviour. Rather than studying each domain in isolation, I enjoy looking for the recurring principles that govern how complex systems organise themselves. That search for universality is one of the most rewarding and thrilling aspects of my research.
    




How did you get into complexity science?

    
    My entry point into complexity science came through my PhD research on geometry-driven hyperuniformity. What began as a study of disordered materials quickly became a fascination with a much broader question: how can remarkably simple local interactions generate striking forms of large-scale order?
    
    
    That experience introduced me to a rich landscape of ideas, including emergence, self-organisation, adaptation, phase transitions, nonlinearity, and collective behaviour, which continue to shape my research today. Although the systems I study have expanded from materials to information, communication, and embodied interaction, the underlying questions have remained remarkably consistent.
    




What is cybernetics? How does it inform your research?

    
    Cybernetics is the study of how systems regulate, adapt, and organise themselves through feedback. Originally developed to understand purposeful behaviour in both living organisms and machines, it has since evolved into a rich way of thinking about complex systems across the natural, social, and technological worlds.
    
    
    What draws me to cybernetics is not simply its concepts, but its way of asking questions. Rather than viewing systems as isolated components, cybernetics encourages us to think in terms of relationships, interactions, feedback loops, adaptation, and emergence. It asks how collective behaviour arises, how systems remain resilient under change, and how they continue to learn and reorganise over time.
    
    
    Voilà, that's what I found in cybernetics: a common language for communicating across fields, connecting research themes from geometry-driven complexity and information dynamics to embodied experiences, such as Musical Allostasis. Cybernetics therefore serves not only as a theoretical foundation, but also as a practical orientation for exploring how complex systems organise, communicate, and evolve.
    




What do you mean by studying information dynamics?


I am interested in how information moves, changes, stabilises, or becomes distorted as it circulates through systems. This includes communication among people, interactions between humans and machines, and the evolving structures through which knowledge is produced, interpreted, and trusted.





Why topology?


Topology offers a way to study shape, structure, and connectivity without reducing a system to isolated parts. I use topological thinking and methods to identify structural signatures in high-dimensional or dynamic systems, especially where meaningful patterns may not be immediately visible.




Teaching and supervision

What kinds of students do you supervise?


I welcome students whose projects engage with complexity, cybernetics, information dynamics, topology, AI-mediated systems, or broader questions about emergence, communication, and knowledge systems. Projects may be computational, conceptual, empirical, design-oriented, or embodied. Above all, I enjoy working with students who are curious, open to crossing disciplinary boundaries, and willing to explore unfamiliar ideas with intellectual generosity.





Do students need a strong mathematical background to work with you?


Preferably, yes. A strong mathematical background is certainly helpful in shaping a project's direction and identifying appropriate analytical approaches. Many of my research projects involve mathematical or computational analysis, so a strong foundation in mathematical reasoning, logic, and intuition can make the work more structured, rigorous, and enjoyable. That said, I also value a willingness to work carefully across methods, assumptions, and levels of abstraction, with curiosity, openness, and attention to detail.





What is your teaching style?


My teaching is grounded in inquiry, reflection, and learning by making (starting from small!). I aim to help students develop conceptual clarity by breaking complex ideas into digestible pieces that can be communicated thoughtfully to diverse audiences. Along the way, I encourage students to learn through toy models, practical tools, prototypes, interactive demonstrations, real-world examples, and situated problems, building confidence not only in understanding complexity but also in explaining it.




Collaboration and public engagement

What kinds of collaborations are you interested in?


I enjoy collaborations that bring together complexity science, cybernetics, natural and artificial intelligence, knowledge systems, communication, education, and creative practice. I am particularly interested in projects where computational, conceptual, or interactive approaches can reveal hidden structures, dynamics, or organising principles. More recently, I have become increasingly interested in developing embodied experiences of complexity, creating ways for people not only to study emergence, but to participate in and experience it firsthand.





Are you available for talks, workshops, or public events?


I am open to invitations that align with my research and teaching interests, particularly around cybernetics, complexity, generative AI, human–AI relations, responsible technology, and topology-informed approaches to understanding systems.





How can I contact you?


The best starting point is either to use the Contact form or to write an email to sungyeon.hong[at]anu.edu.au. For supervision or collaboration enquiries, it is helpful to include a brief description of the topic, context, and what kind of conversation or outcome you have in mind.




Me-human

How do you pronounce your name?


    Many people find my name difficult to pronounce (sometimes I do too!) and often misspell it by adding a mysterious "g" at the end. Here's a simple trick.
    I love singing. The verb "sing" becomes "sang" and then "sung". Say the last one again: That's exactly how the first part of my name sounds!
    The second part is "yeon", which is shorter than "yawn" and lighter than "young". 
    Now, put them together and you get **Sung-yeon** (which is **성연** in Korean). Don't worry if you don't get it right the first time — I respond to a surprising number of variations. :)





What do you do for fun?


    Outside work, I enjoy drawing, cooking (+ eating), gardening, hiking, travelling, playing music and singing, watching French comedies, and spending time with my family and doggos. Sport-wise, I love racquet sports, especially squash and badminton. It just feels as though I've grown wings whenever I have a racquet in my hand!





What languages do you speak?


My mother tongue is Korean, which I am continually trying to keep up with its ever-evolving modern forms while living abroad. I speak French, can read German, can produce a surprisingly convincing Italian accents (thanks to my Italian/Swiss-Italian amici), and have a patchy understanding of Chinese. Languages fascinate me, as each offers a different way of seeing and describing the world. As an ongoing stretch goal, I am also a keen listener to our fellow doggos and babies, both of whom seem to communicate far more than they are often given credit for.





This FAQ is intentionally informal and evolving. I expect to update it as my research, teaching, and collaborations continue to develop, along with my own self. :)

  About
  
    
      
    
    
      
        I am a Lecturer at the School of Cybernetics, Australian National University (ANU), in Canberra, Australia.
      
      
        My research sits at the intersection of complexity science, cybernetics, topology, and information dynamics. I study how structure emerges, evolves, and sometimes degrades in systems composed of many interacting parts from geometric point patterns to human–AI communication systems and knowledge landscapes.
      
      
        Across these projects, I use topology not only as a mathematical toolkit, but as a way of seeing: a means of identifying shapes, holes, flows, and structural signatures that reveal how local interactions give rise to global phenomena.

          Begin with the default state, then vary a single initial condition, parameter, or local rule. Observe not only what changes, but also what remains stable. Repeating this process helps reveal feedback, thresholds, path dependence, robustness, and other signatures of complex behaviour.

text:
← Resources Overview
  Concepts · Methods · Shared vocabulary
  Glossary
  
    
      Cybernetics and complexity science are inherently multidisciplinary. Their ideas move between mathematics, physics, biology, computer science, social science, design, and other fields, often carrying slightly different meanings or emphases with them.
    
    
      This glossary provides concise working introductions to core concepts and to established or emerging methods that appear across my research, teaching, and writing. It is not intended as an exhaustive dictionary. Rather, it offers a shared vocabulary for navigating the website and for seeing how ideas that originate in different disciplines can become connected.
    
  



  
    
      
        Concept constellation
        How the ideas connect
      
      
        Select a term to reveal neighbouring concepts that share one or more tags. The links indicate conceptual overlap rather than equivalence or a formal dependency.
      
    

    
      Adaptation
      Agent-based modelling
      Allostasis
      Attractor
      Complexity science
      Criticality
      Phase transition
      Cybernetics
      Emergence
      Feedback
      Feedforward
      Hyperuniformity
      Persistent homology
      
                Scaling
            
      Self-organisation
      Topology
      Universality
    

    
      Select a term to highlight related ideas.
    
    Reset connections
  



  
    
      Working definitions
      Browse the glossary
    
    
      Find a term
      
    
  

  

    
      
        Adaptation
        A change in behaviour, structure, or organisation in response to conditions encountered over time.
        
      
      
        In complex systems, adaptation may occur at the level of individual components, interactions, or the collective itself. The important question is often not simply whether a system changes, but what information it uses, what it retains from the past, and what remains stable while it changes.
        dynamicscyberneticsfeedbackregulation
      
    

    
      
        Agent-based modelling
        A computational approach that represents individual agents and their local rules to study collective behaviour.
        
      
      
        Rather than prescribing a system's large-scale behaviour directly, an agent-based model specifies how individual entities act and interact. Repeated simulation then reveals what macroscopic patterns, regularities, or unexpected behaviours can emerge from those rules.
        methodsimulationagentsemergence
      
    

    
      
        Allostasis
        The maintenance of stability through change, including adaptive and anticipatory regulation.
        
      
      
        Allostasis shifts attention away from returning to one fixed state and towards maintaining viability as conditions change. On this website, the idea is particularly useful for thinking about systems that respond to current conditions while also anticipating what may happen next.
        adaptationanticipationregulationembodiment
      
    

    
      
        Attractor
        A state or set of states towards which a dynamical system tends to evolve after transient behaviour.
        
      
      
        Attractors provide one way of describing the long-term organisation of dynamics. Depending on the system, an attractor may be a fixed point, a repeating cycle, or a more complicated set of states.
        dynamicsstate-spacenonlinear systems
      
    

    
      
        Complexity science
        The study of systems whose collective behaviour arises from many interacting components and cannot be understood from the components alone.
        
      
      
        Complexity science asks how interactions, feedback, heterogeneity, adaptation, and history produce organisation across scales. Its methods span analytical models, simulation, network analysis, statistical physics, data-driven approaches, and qualitative inquiry.
        complex systemsemergencedynamicsinterdisciplinarity
      
    

    
      
        Criticality
        Behaviour associated with the vicinity of a transition where fluctuations and correlations can extend across many scales.
        
      
      
        Near a critical point, systems can become unusually sensitive to perturbations and may display scaling behaviour or long-range correlations. The concept originates in statistical physics but has also inspired broader approaches to biological, computational, and social systems.
        phase transitionscalingfluctuationsuniversalitycomplexity science
      
    

    
      
        Cybernetics
        A transdisciplinary field concerned with communication, feedback, control, regulation, and purposeful behaviour in systems.
        
      
      
        Cybernetics studies how systems sense, communicate, act, and regulate themselves or one another. Rather than belonging to one application domain, its concepts have travelled across engineering, biology, cognition, organisations, design, and social systems.
        feedbackregulationcommunicationcontrol
      
    

    
      
        Emergence
        The appearance of collective patterns or properties that arise from interactions among components.
        
      
      
        An emergent pattern need not be explicitly represented in the rules followed by individual components. The concept is therefore central to understanding how simple local interactions can produce organised behaviour at a larger scale.
        complex systemsself-organisationlocal rulescollective behaviour
      
    

    
      
        Feedback
        A process in which the consequences of an action or state influence what the system does next.
        
      
      
        Feedback can stabilise, amplify, or reorganise behaviour depending on how information is returned and acted upon. It is a foundational concept in cybernetics and a recurring mechanism across biological, technological, ecological, and social systems.
        cyberneticsregulationadaptationdynamics
      
    

    
      
        Feedforward
        Anticipatory action taken in response to an expected change rather than only to an observed error.
        
      
      
        Where feedback responds to consequences that are already observable, feedforward uses a model, cue, or expectation about what is likely to happen. The distinction is useful when studying adaptive systems that combine reaction with anticipation.
        cyberneticsanticipationregulationallostasis
      
    

    
      
        Hyperuniformity
        A form of large-scale order characterised by unusually suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations.
        
      
      
        Hyperuniform systems can be disordered at short distances while becoming strongly constrained at large scales. This makes hyperuniformity useful for studying forms of order that lie between conventional categories such as crystals and ordinary disordered materials.
        spatial orderfluctuationsgeometrystatistical physics
      
    

    
      
        Persistent homology
        A topological data analysis method that tracks features such as connected components and loops across scale.
        
      
      
        Instead of choosing one scale in advance, persistent homology asks when topological features appear and disappear as a scale parameter changes. Features that persist across a wide range of scales are often interpreted as more structurally significant than short-lived ones. Try this interactive demo to get a sense of how persistent homology works.
        methodtopologydata analysisscale
      
    
    
    
            
                Phase transition

                
                  A qualitative change in a system's collective state that occurs when a control parameter crosses a threshold.
                

                
            

            
                
                  A phase transition occurs when a system changes from one macroscopic state or regime to another as some condition is varied. Familiar physical examples include water freezing into ice or a magnet losing its magnetisation as temperature changes. In complex systems, the idea is used more broadly to describe abrupt or qualitative changes in collective organisation, behaviour, or connectivity.
                

                
                  Near a transition point, small changes in local interactions can sometimes produce large-scale changes across the whole system. This makes phase transitions closely related to ideas such as criticality, emergence, collective behaviour, and scaling.
                

                
                  complexity
                  dynamics
                  criticality
                  emergence
                  statistical mechanics
                
            
        
        
        
            
                Scaling

                
                  A relationship in which the behaviour or structure of a system changes systematically with scale, often following simple mathematical laws.
                

                
            

            
                
                  Scaling describes how a quantity changes as the size, resolution, distance, time scale, or some other characteristic scale of a system is varied. In many complex systems, these relationships can be expressed through power laws, where the same mathematical form persists across a range of scales.
                

                
                  Scaling is closely associated with criticality and phase transitions, where systems may develop correlations across many different length or time scales and lose a single characteristic scale. Similar scaling behaviour can sometimes appear in otherwise very different systems, which is one reason the concept is also closely connected to universality.
                

                
                  criticality
                  phase transition
                  universality
                  power law
                  self-similarity
                  statistical physics
                
            
        

    
      
        Self-organisation
        The formation or maintenance of collective organisation through local interactions without a central controller specifying the global pattern.
        
      
      
        Self-organisation does not imply the absence of constraints, environments, or external influences. It describes how coordination at one scale can arise through interactions occurring at another.
        emergencelocal rulescollective behaviourdynamics
      
    

    
      
        Topology
        The mathematics of qualitative structure, including properties such as connectivity and holes that persist under continuous deformation.
        
      
      
        Topology provides a language for describing structure without depending on exact distances or angles. In data analysis, this perspective can help identify robust organisation that may be difficult to see using purely metric or coordinate-based descriptions.
        mathematicsconnectivityshapedata analysis
      
    

    
      
        Universality
        The appearance of the same large-scale behaviour in systems whose microscopic details can be very different.
        
      
      
        Universality is especially important in the theory of critical phenomena, where systems with different constituents can share the same scaling laws. More broadly, it motivates the search for structural principles that survive changes in microscopic implementation.
        scalingcriticalitystatistical physicspatterns

title: AI and Productivity
text:
It is indeed an important question whether AI is genuinely contributing to an increase in net productivity of human society. In my view, this touches on many different aspects of society, not economics alone, as the impact of AI use and its integration into our daily activities and organisations is so broad, spanning politics, economics, research sectors, education, and even human psychology.
I suppose the relationship between the performance of AI models and human productivity is highly non-linear; hence the use of the term “net” productivity. Considering the multi-dimensional nature of AI’s influence on human society, productivity may be more appropriately modelled as a vector-valued quantity, rather than a single scalar quantity.
For me, intelligence itself is a double-edged sword (if not multi-edged!). Intelligence can be seen as the product of an agent’s evolution (whether living or non-living) to maximise the utility of surrounding resources in order to sustain its own existence. It manifests at many different levels, from cells to organisms to collectives. However, intelligence does not necessarily lead to outcomes that optimise long-term sustainment or performance. For example, highly optimised systems can become brittle: financial markets driven by sophisticated algorithms can amplify instability, or individuals may overfit to short-term gains at the expense of long-term well-being. In this sense, intelligence can both enhance and undermine the very goals it appears to serve.
In such a way, intelligence, as an entity, can be viewed as a complex system. This leads me to wonder whether the very question of mapping AI (as a form of intelligence) to (economic) productivity is well-defined. This resembles attempting to define a function between two spaces whose dimensions and metrics are themselves evolving. If both “intelligence” and “productivity” are multi-dimensional, context-dependent, and dynamically evolving, then any attempt to establish a stable, one-to-one mapping between them may be inherently reductive. At best, we may only capture partial projections of this relationship under specific assumptions or time scales.
On top of that, intelligence is often reduced to a single scalar metric, but I do not believe that tells the whole story when evaluating an agent’s performance. By bringing this up, I think the point I am making is that AI is not simply a tool that linearly increases/decreases productivity. Rather, it reshapes the structure of productivity itself: redistributing effort, attention, and value across different dimensions, some of which may not be immediately visible or measurable.
From an economic perspective, this raises questions about how we even define and measure productivity in the presence of AI. For instance, conventional measures such as total factor productivity (TFP) attempt to capture efficiency gains that are not explained by inputs like labour and capital. However, if AI fundamentally alters what counts as “labour”, augments cognitive processes, and reorganises workflows, then TFP may be capturing only a shadow of these transformations rather than their full substance.
Moreover, the impact of AI is unlikely to be confined to local improvements in efficiency. Through general equilibrium effects, gains in one sector may induce shifts in others, changing demand structures, labour allocation, and even the nature of tasks themselves. In this sense, productivity is not merely increased but “reconfigured” across the system.
This also connects to innovation dynamics: AI may accelerate certain forms of innovation while constraining or displacing others, depending on how it channels attention and resources. As such, the question is not only whether AI increases net productivity, but also what kinds of productivity it privileges, and over what time scales. Some gains may appear immediately, while others, such as losses in diversity, resilience, or long-term adaptability, may only become visible later.
Rather than asking “Does AI increase productivity?”, the question may have to be whether our current conceptual and measurement frameworks are adequate to even recognise the kinds of changes it brings, like in many other questions. (And yes, I am rerouting a question once again! And I guess I will keep doing so quite often for a reason.)
What I found particularly resonant is that these questions around productivity are not entirely separate from my earlier reflections on relationality, boundary, and alienation in the context of AI. If AI lacks relationality in the sense of being situated within lived, experiential networks, then its contribution to “productivity” may also be relationally incomplete, optimising along dimensions that are legible within data, while leaving out those that emerge through human context, meaning, and consequence.
At the same time, the blurring boundary between human and AI complicates this further: if our activities are already entangled with AI systems, then productivity itself becomes a hybrid construct, no longer attributable to either side alone. Yet, as noted in the sense of foreignness or alienation, this entanglement does not fully dissolve the distinction. We simultaneously experience integration and separation. This tension suggests that what we call productivity may itself sit within this dual condition: partially shared, partially disjoint, and not easily reducible to a single measure.
This makes me wonder whether productivity, much like relationality, is not an intrinsic property of a system, but something that emerges through relations — relations that AI may simulate but not fully inhabit.
